# 2 Samuel Chapter 14 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 183v–184v | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/2SA_014_page_001.jpg, 2SA_014_page_002.jpg, 2SA_014_page_003.jpg

---

**1** Joab son of Zeruiah could see that the king's heart longed for Absalom. **2** So Joab sent to Tekoa and brought back a woman known for her wisdom. He told her, "I need you to act as if you're in mourning. Put on funeral clothes. Don't use any perfume. Make yourself look like a woman who has been grieving for the dead a long time. **3** Then go to the king and say exactly what I tell you." And Joab coached her on every word.

**4** The woman from Tekoa went to the king. She fell facedown on the ground and cried out, "Help me, your majesty!"

**5** "What's the matter?" the king asked. She said, "I'm a widow, sir. My husband is dead. **6** I had two sons. They got into a fight out in the field — no one was there to break it up — and one of them struck the other and killed him. **7** Now the whole family has turned against me. They're demanding, 'Hand over the one who killed his brother! We'll execute him to pay for his brother's life — and we'll wipe out the heir while we're at it.' They want to snuff out my last glowing ember — the only one left to carry on my husband's name in this world."

**8** The king said, "Go home. I'll take care of this for you."

**9** The woman said, "My lord the king, let any blame fall on me and my father's house. The king and his throne are innocent."

**10** The king said, "If anyone gives you trouble, bring him to me. He won't bother you again."

**11** She pressed further: "Please, let the king swear by the LORD your God that the blood-avenger won't add to the destruction and kill my son." He said, "As the LORD lives, not a single hair of your son's head will fall to the ground."

**12** Then the woman said, "May your servant say one more thing to my lord the king?" He said, "Go ahead."

**13** The woman said, "Then why have you done the very same thing against the people of God? By this ruling, the king condemns himself — because the king has not brought home his own banished son.

**14** We all die eventually. We're like water poured out on the ground — you can't scoop it back up. But God doesn't just snatch life away. Instead, he makes plans to bring the outcast home.

**15** The reason I came to speak to the king about this is that people threatened me, and I thought, 'I'll go to the king — maybe he'll do what I ask. **16** The king will listen and rescue his servant from the man who wants to cut off both me and my son from the inheritance God gave us.'

**17** I told myself, 'The word of my lord the king will put my mind at ease.' For my lord the king is like an angel of God in telling right from wrong. May the LORD your God be with you."

**18** The king answered her, "I want you to be completely honest with me about something." She said, "Ask anything, my lord."

**19** "Was Joab behind this — all of it?" the king asked. The woman answered, "As surely as you live, my lord the king, there's no getting around what you've said. Yes — it was your servant Joab. He instructed me. He put every one of these words in my mouth. **20** He did it to approach the matter from a different angle. But my lord is wise — wise as an angel of God — and knows everything that happens in the land."

**21** The king turned to Joab and said, "Very well, I will do this. Go and bring the young man Absalom back."

**22** Joab fell facedown to the ground, bowed low, and blessed the king. "Today," Joab said, "your servant knows he has found favor with you, my lord — because the king has done what his servant asked."

**23** Joab set out for Geshur and brought Absalom back to Jerusalem.

**24** But the king said, "He may return to his own house, but he is not to see my face." So Absalom went to his house and did not see the king.

**25** In all of Israel, no one was more admired for his appearance than Absalom. From the bottom of his feet to the top of his head, he was flawless. **26** When he cut his hair — which he did once a year because the weight of it became too much — the hair weighed five pounds by the royal standard.

**27** Absalom had three sons and one daughter. He named the daughter Tamar. She grew up to be a beautiful woman.

**28** Absalom lived in Jerusalem for two full years and never once saw the king's face.

**29** He sent for Joab, wanting him to go to the king on his behalf, but Joab refused to come. He sent again — still Joab wouldn't come. **30** So Absalom told his servants, "You see Joab's barley field, right next to mine? Go set it on fire." And they did.

**31** That got Joab moving. He went straight to Absalom's house. "Why did your servants burn my field?" he demanded.

**32** Absalom said, "I sent for you to come so I could send you to the king with a question: 'Why did I bother coming back from Geshur? I'd be better off still there!' Let me see the king face to face. If I'm guilty of something, let him execute me."

**33** Joab went to the king and relayed the message. The king summoned Absalom. He came and bowed down with his face to the ground before the king. And the king kissed Absalom.

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**Verse 1 — Joab reads the room:** The Hebrew says Joab "knew" (*vayeda'*) that the king's heart was "upon" (*'al*) Absalom. Joab is a master manipulator throughout 2 Samuel — a man whose loyalty to David is genuine but whose methods are relentlessly pragmatic. He sees David's longing and designs a scheme to exploit it.

**Verse 7 — "my last glowing ember":** The Hebrew *gachalti* — "my coal" — is one of the most heartbreaking metaphors in the Old Testament. A single coal, still glowing in the ashes, can rekindle a family. The clan wants to stamp it out. The woman is arguing for the survival of a lineage — and by extension, so is Joab, arguing for the survival of the royal line through Absalom.

**Verse 14 — the theological pivot:** This is the heart of the wise woman's argument, and it is genuinely profound: human life is fragile (water poured out), death is irreversible, but God himself acts to bring back those who have been cast out. The word *niddach* (banished one/outcast) carries the weight of exile theology. If God works to restore the outcast, the king — God's representative — should do the same.

**Verse 24 — the half-measure:** David allows Absalom to return but refuses to see him. This is the worst possible outcome: close enough to be tantalizing, far enough to be humiliating. Absalom has the geography of restoration without the relationship. Two years of this limbo will harden into the resentment that fuels the rebellion.

**Verse 27 — naming her Tamar:** Absalom names his daughter after his violated sister. This is not a casual choice — it is a memorial, a permanent marker of unresolved injustice. Every time he called his daughter's name, he spoke the name of the wrong that was never made right.

**Verse 30 — the burning field:** Absalom's decision to burn Joab's barley field is both absurd and revealing. It shows his characteristic combination of audacity and impatience. He cannot wait. He will not be ignored. This is the same personality that will soon attempt to seize a kingdom.

*— PNEUMA*
